059:1: During the two hundred and fifty million years in which the sea cradled and nurtured life, through what stages did life finish preparing to step out onto the land?
059:4: In Paper 58 we heard how the Life Carriers planted the first life in three seas five hundred and fifty million years ago. Now Paper 59 follows the long age in which that life grew and diversified in the sea. The author is a Life Carrier of the original corps assigned to Urantia (59:6.13).
059:5: The author divides about one billion years of Urantia history into five eras. Of these, the marine-life era covers two hundred and fifty million years—about one quarter of the planet's history—and is divided into six long periods (59:0.1-0.7). At the opening of this era the sea bottoms and continental shelves were covered with prolific vegetation, and the stage was set for the first chapters of the great stone book (59:0.8).
059:6: How, then, did life advance from the trilobites to the fishes and frogs, and why did this era end in biologic tribulation?
059:8: The sea mothered and nurtured the early life of the realm. (59:6.12)
059:32: When this era opened, life existed only in the inland seas and along the shore lines; there was as yet no land life (59:1.1). By four hundred million years ago marine life had spread over the whole world, and vegetation was beginning for the first time to creep out onto the land (59:1.2-1.3). Then suddenly, with no gradual ancestral line, the first multicellular animals, the trilobites, appeared and ruled the seas for ages (59:1.4).
059:39: Shallow water where waves prevented mud from settling
059:45: The climate then was oceanic, and the warm Gulf Stream bathed Greenland, making today's continent of ice a tropical paradise (59:1.17). Trilobites grew from two inches to a foot long and were divided into carnivorous, herbivorous, omnivorous, and mud-eating kinds. That they were the last multicellular animals able to live on inorganic matter explains their abundance (59:1.19). This fifty-million-year period is the Cambrian (59:1.20).
059:47: The rising and sinking of the land in this era were all slow and undramatic. The Asiatic mother continent did not fully share the history of the other continents, and in recent ages it has become the most stable land (59:2.1).
059:52: The great flooding of all continents except central Asia begins
059:54: Sinking again — the age of great limestone deposits
059:56: A quiet period; great volcanic eruptions in eastern Kentucky
059:58: The third great flood; eastern North America and western Europe deeply submerged
059:60: The Mexican uplift forms the Gulf Sea
059:62: This period saw great evolution of individual animal organisms. Marine animals developed so far that every type below the vertebrates appears in the fossils, but there was still too much carbon dioxide in the air for land animals (59:2.9). The trilobites flourished in tens of thousands of patterns, and cephalopods, gastropods, bivalves, and brachiopods appeared in forms almost the same as today (59:2.10-2.12). This period is the Ordovician (59:2.13).
059:64: Three hundred million years ago another submergence began, and creatures with limy shells laid down the first extensive limestone layers, averaging a thousand feet thick (59:3.1). Two hundred and ninety million years ago early mountain movements began, such as the Himalayas and the great Caledonian range, and the deposits of this age yield much gas, oil, zinc, and lead (59:3.3-3.4).
059:65: The trilobites declined rapidly, and cephalopods growing up to fifteen feet long suddenly appeared and became masters of the sea (59:3.5). The rock laid down by the submergence of two hundred and eighty million years ago is the Niagara limestone, over which Niagara Falls flows today (59:3.9). Toward the end of this age the primitive water scorpions evolved, and soon after, suddenly, the scorpions appeared—the first true air-breathing animals (59:3.11). These twenty-five million years are the Silurian (59:3.12).
059:67: Now came an age in which, in the long struggle between land and sea, the land prevailed. The bare landscape was clothed in green, and the first magnificent forests appeared (59:4.1-4.2). Two hundred and seventy million years ago was one of the greatest land-emergence epochs in all world history (59:4.4).
059:68: The greatest event of this age was the sudden appearance of the fishes. When the first vertebrates of the animal kingdom appeared in the north two hundred and fifty million years ago, their forerunners, the modified arthropods, quickly disappeared (59:4.9-4.10). Today's sharks are survivors of these ancient fishes (59:4.11). On land the ferns suddenly appeared in great numbers and spread, and the forests of leafless trees were silent forests, without even a rustle (59:4.13, 4.17).
059:75: A long body joining head and tail / jawless pre-fishes
059:77: Fishes — appearing suddenly, while the forerunners soon died out
059:79: This age of fishes, lasting almost fifty million years, is the Devonian (59:4.18).
059:81: The appearance of the fishes was the peak of marine-life evolution, and from now on the evolution of land life becomes ever more important (59:5.1). Two hundred and ten million years ago, when the seas were at their widest, the first land animals suddenly appeared: air-breathing amphibians came from arthropods whose swim bladders had evolved into lungs (59:5.5). Snails, scorpions, and frogs crawled out of the sea onto the land, and frogs still lay their eggs in water (59:5.6).
059:82: Insects soon appeared and spread, and dragonflies had wings measuring thirty inches across (59:5.7). From two hundred million years ago true coal formation went on for more than twenty-five million years. Coal is the luxuriant vegetation of swamps, preserved by water and transformed by pressure, and the tree roots left intact in the clay beneath the coal beds show that it formed right where it lies (59:5.13, 5.16).
059:85: Times of sinking and rising shown by coal layers
059:95: The Carboniferous period ended one hundred and eighty million years ago, and as the land rose, the mild oceanic climate began to change into a more variable continental climate (59:5.20-5.21). The life of the coal age was marked by ferns and frogs (59:5.23).
059:97: This was an age of great impoverishment of life. More than a hundred thousand species at the end of the marine-life era had dwindled to fewer than five hundred by the close of this transition period (59:6.2). The cause was not catastrophe but a combination of ordinary influences—the narrowing of the seas and the great uplift of the land. The mild oceanic climate disappeared, and new climatic factors, glacial action and aridity, appeared (59:6.3, 6.6).

059:104: Evolve dormant stages to survive winter and drought
059:106: Decline, yet in Africa take the first step toward the reptiles
059:108: Take refuge in three havens: the Mexican Gulf, the Ganges Bay, and the Sicilian Bay
059:110: By one hundred and sixty million years ago the land was covered with vegetation, and the atmosphere had become suitable for animal respiration. This tribulation left only life with survival value, qualifying it to become the ancestor of the more rapidly developing life of the next age (59:6.10). The close of this Permian period brings the Paleozoic era to an end (59:6.11).

059:115: Paper 59 tells the story of the sea over two hundred and fifty million years in six periods. The land sank and rose countless times, and each time a new page was laid down in the rocks. New life usually appeared suddenly, and at the end of the era a severe tribulation left only life with survival value. The sea cradled and nurtured life like a mother until the land was ready to receive it, and now, its role fulfilled, it hands the second stage of evolution over to the land.

060:1: Why did the giant dinosaurs disappear, and how did the hundred million years ruled by the reptiles open a path of evolution in which not bodies but brains would grow?
060:4: In Paper 59 we saw the sea cradle and nurture life for two hundred and fifty million years and then, after a severe tribulation, hand its role over to the land. Now Paper 60 takes up the hundred million years in which land life dominated—the Mesozoic era. The author is a Life Carrier of Nebadon now active on Urantia (60:4.7).
060:5: The age of exclusively marine life was over. As the land rose, as the crust and the seas cooled, and as the seas narrowed and deepened, the climate of regions far from the equator changed greatly (60:0.1). The frogs, masters of the previous age, survived in greatly reduced numbers, and even the spore-bearing plants had almost disappeared (60:0.2).
060:6: On this new stage, then, how did the reptiles rise and decline, and how did flowers, birds, and mountains meanwhile prepare the world we know today?
060:8: ⟦Q 60:2.14⟧Henceforth, evolution will follow the growth of brains, not physical bulk, and the development of brains will characterize each succeeding epoch of animal evolution and planetary progress.⟦/Q⟧ (60:2.14)

Fossils are scarce, but many sandstone footprints of land reptiles remain, and land animals carried on only in certain regions of Africa (60:1.1-1.2). The early land-life era began one hundred and fifty million years ago. Life was not abundant, but it fared better than at the harsh close of the marine-life era (60:1.5).
060:13: One hundred and forty million years ago the reptiles suddenly appeared, fully developed. They soon gave rise to crocodiles, scaled reptiles, sea serpents, and flying reptiles, while their transitional ancestors quickly disappeared (60:1.9). The dinosaurs soon became the monarchs of this age. They were unlike all other animals in moving bodies of up to forty tons with brains weighing less than a pound (60:1.10).

060:20: Walking on all fours; one branch developed protective armor

060:24: The greatest event of this period, which began one hundred and twenty million years ago, was the evolution and decline of the dinosaurs. They evolved in every size, from species less than two feet long to huge herbivores seventy-five feet long (60:2.1). But the bigger they grew, the more sluggish and weak they became; they needed enormous amounts of food but lacked the intelligence to cope, and so they literally starved to death and disappeared (60:2.3).
060:28: Two species that went to the water (sea serpents, ichthyosaurs)
060:29: Evolutionary retrogression — fifty feet long with brains under two ounces; they perished
060:31: Always returned to the land to lay their eggs
060:32: Two types that went to the air (pterosaurs)

060:41: The Cretaceous takes its name from the foraminifers that make chalk in the sea. In this period the dominance of the reptiles draws to a close, flowering plants and birds appear, and continental drift comes to a stop (60:3.1). As the westward-drifting continents struck the bed of the Pacific, the great north-south mountain range stretching from Alaska to Cape Horn began to rise. The age of modern mountain building had begun (60:3.2-3.3).

060:56: One of the greatest lava flows in history

These seed-bearing plants were to the plant world what the ancestors of man were to the animal world, second in evolutionary importance only to the appearance of man himself (60:3.19).
060:66: Second: bird-like creatures that walked and swam in the water
060:69: Came directly from the reptiles and became the ancestors of all birds

The alternating dominance of land and sea has gone on in cycles of about a million years, and this rhythm will continue, though it will become ever rarer and smaller (60:4.1).
060:73: The most basic factor determining where mountains form is not the pressure of the continents but old lowlands filled with light deposits—the zones of depression. When the crust comes under pressure, these lighter areas crumple and rise first (60:4.2).

060:80: The second European east-west system, formed about the same time as the Pacific rim
060:82: The Rocky Mountain system — eroded, then raised again and carved anew
060:84: By the end of this period the fern forests had largely given way to modern trees such as the giant redwoods. There were still no placental mammals, but the stage was fully set for the ancestors of the mammals to appear in the next age (60:4.5). With the fifty-million-year Cretaceous, the hundred-million-year Mesozoic era comes to an end (60:4.6).
060:86: Paper 60 shows how the age of giant bodies came to an end. The reptiles appeared suddenly and took over the land, the sea, and even the sky, but lacking brains to match their bulk, they could not feed themselves and disappeared. The lines that returned to the sea retrogressed, and the two attempts to fly failed. Yet meanwhile flowering plants and seed-bearing grasses covered the world, true birds appeared, and as continental drift halted, today's mountain ranges rose. The lesson of this long age is clear: from now on evolution moves forward by the growth not of bodies but of brains, and at the end of that road stands man.

061:1: How did the mammals, which care for their young and use their brains, take over the world, and how was man born in the frozen ice age?
061:4: In Paper 60 we saw the age of the dinosaurs—giant bodies without intelligence—come to an end, and evolution begin to follow the growth of brains. Now Paper 61 takes up the age of the mammals, who stood on that road. It covers a little less than fifty million years, from the appearance of the placental mammals to the end of the ice age (61:0.1). This story was sponsored by a resident Life Carrier (61:7.20).
061:5: During this Cenozoic era the world was an enchanting landscape of rolling hills, broad valleys, great rivers, and forests—an animal paradise with trees full of birds (61:0.2). The deposits laid down over five periods hold the fossils of successive mammalian dynasties, and the record leads straight up to the time when mankind actually appeared (61:0.3).
061:6: By what advantages, then, did the mammals take over the world, and how did the ice age that came at the end fit together with the birth of man?
061:8: ⟦Q 61:2.5⟧Brains and agility had replaced armor and size in the progress of animal survival.⟦/Q⟧ (61:2.5)
061:12: Fifty million years ago the placental mammals suddenly appeared in North America. This was the most important evolutionary development up to that time. Their father was a small, active, carnivorous leaping dinosaur that had survived through the period of dinosaur decline (61:1.2). In these primitive mammals the basic mammalian instincts began to show themselves (61:1.3).
061:19: Feeding, raising, and protecting them with affectionate care
061:21: Using superior brain power for self-perpetuation
061:25: Using superior intelligence for environmental adjustment and adaptation
061:27: Forty-five million years ago small horses, rhinoceroses, tapirs, primitive pigs, lemurs, and monkeys lived in the forests, and a ten-foot ostrich-like bird was the ancestor of the great passenger birds that later carried men through the air (61:1.9). The mammals of this period were all covered with hair and had brains large for their bodies, but none of the modern forms had yet appeared (61:1.10). This period is called the Eocene (61:1.14).
061:29: From thirty-five million years ago the placental mammals began to rule the world (61:2.3). Over a hundred species of primitive mammals died out, and the mammals of large size and small brain soon perished too. As the dinosaurs declined, the mammals took over the earth and completely displaced the remainder of their reptilian ancestors (61:2.5). Of the old reptiles, only the turtles, snakes, and crocodiles survived, along with the frogs (61:2.6).
061:30: Thirty million years ago modern types of mammals began to appear. From mountain-dwelling mammals the grazing hoofed animals of the plains branched off, and the camel and llama originated in North America (61:2.8-2.9). In western North America the ancestors of the line from which the true lemurs would later come first appeared (61:2.10). As the snakes had done, one group of mammals left the land and went to the sea, becoming whales, dolphins, seals, and sea lions (61:2.11). This ten-million-year period is the Oligocene (61:2.13).
061:32: Twenty million years ago was truly the golden age of the mammals. Mastodons and many cats came from Asia to North America over the Bering Strait land bridge, and deer and ruminants filled the plains (61:3.4-3.5). For once the world was ruled by an animal with a brain large enough to match its huge body—the elephant (61:3.6).
061:37: A large body, a fine brain, and emotional control — but its size left it lacking in agility
061:39: Second only to the elephant in quality of brain — but could not overcome its tendency to flee when frightened
061:41: The only being who surpasses the elephant in intelligence and adaptability
061:43: The author urges that, as we enter the so-called “horseless age,” we pause to consider what the horse meant to our ancestors, having long served mankind for food, travel, agriculture, and war (61:3.11). In central Asia true types of monkeys and gorillas evolved, but they have no connection with the ancestral line of mankind (61:3.12). This period is the Miocene (61:3.15).
061:45: In this period just before the ice age, mountain ranges formed and rivers changed their courses, and Mounts Shasta, Hood, and Rainier began their careers as mountains (61:4.1-4.2). For a time all the lands except Australia were joined again, and the last great animal migration took place (61:4.3).
061:55: Horses (in their present form five million years ago)
061:58: As the climate cooled, the northern land bridge sank and the connection between Africa and South America was broken, so the eastern and western hemispheres each began to foster their own distinctive life (61:4.6). By the end of this Pliocene period of about ten million years, the ancestors of man had still not appeared (61:4.7).
061:60: The lands of northeastern North America and northern Europe rose greatly, and as ocean currents and seasonal winds shifted, snow fell almost continuously on the northern highlands. It piled up to a depth of 20,000 feet and became creeping ice (61:5.1-5.2). The ice sheets lay not on today's mountain regions but on the elevated highlands (61:5.3).
061:71: The northern regions suffered six distinct glacial invasions (61:5.4). Two million years ago the first glacier advanced southward as far as Kansas, and a million and a half years ago the second invasion began (61:5.5-5.6). In the early ice age North America teemed with animals such as mastodons, woolly mammoths, and saber-toothed tigers, but as the cold deepened, most of them disappeared (61:5.7). Glaciation was, after all, a local phenomenon, so life far from the ice changed little (61:5.8).
061:73: The most important event of the ice age was the evolution of primitive man. In land west of India, now under water, the dawn mammals suddenly appeared among the descendants of the North American lemur type (61:6.1). The road to man ran through a series of sudden mutations.

061:92: The glaciers left marks on the land unlike those of any other phenomenon—moraines, drumlins, and boulders (61:7.1). The advances of the glaciers also line up in time with the history of mankind.

This ice age of more than two million years is the Pleistocene (61:7.17).
061:113: Paper 61 carries the fifty-million-year story of the mammals up to the birth of man. The secret of the mammals' conquest of the world was not armor or size but brains, agility, and the affection that cares for the young. The elephant and the horse showed the power of those brains, and after the last great migration the continents each fostered their own life. Then, in the harshest time, as the world was being covered with ice, two primitive humans were born at the end of a series of sudden mutations. Our ancestors grew up not in a comfortable paradise but in a stimulating and difficult environment, and the chronology of the ice age runs side by side with the human story of the six colored races, the Planetary Prince, the Lucifer rebellion, and the arrival of Adam.

062:1: How did the first human beings, able to worship and to choose, come forth from a small lemur line?
062:4: In Paper 61 we saw how, through the age of the mammals, the continents, the climate, and animal life were made ready as a stage to receive man. Now Paper 62 takes up the scene in which man at last appears on that stage. About one million years ago the immediate ancestors of mankind appeared, through three successive and sudden mutations, from an early line of the lemur type of placental mammal (62:0.1).
062:5: The basis of this line came from the western, or American, group of life plasm, but it was strengthened by contributions from the central life implantation, which had evolved in Africa. The eastern life group contributed little to the production of the human species (62:0.1). This paper is told as the story a Life Carrier of Nebadon, resident on Urantia, witnessed firsthand (62:7.8).
062:6: What, then, was the road from the dawn mammals through the mid-mammals and the Primates to the first human beings? And when did the universe recognize this planet as a world inhabited by man?
062:8: This is the first decision of mind—the human type of mind—on Urantia and automatically establishes the circuit of communication. (62:7.3)

062:13: Millions of years ago the North American type of lemur crossed the Bering land bridge and slowly made its way southwest along the coasts of Asia. Reaching the pleasant lands west of India, it blended with other favorable strains, and there the ancestral strain of mankind was established (62:1.2). Later, as the coasts sank, this Mesopotamian or Persian peninsula became an isolated paradise with no way in or out except to the north, and from it came two groups: the modern simian tribes and the human species (62:1.3).

062:27: A little over a million years ago the Mesopotamian dawn mammals suddenly appeared. They were hairy, agile creatures about three feet tall; they could stand upright with ease and chattered like monkeys, but unlike the simian tribes they ate meat. They had a primitive opposable thumb and a grasping great toe (62:2.1). From about this time the human line went on developing the thumb while losing the grasping power of the great toe, and the simian line did the opposite.
062:28: For their size they had larger brains than any animal of their day, and they already showed many of the emotions of later primitive man (62:2.3). Keenly alert to the dangers of the forest, they built shelters high in the trees, and this is where mankind's tendency to fear began (62:2.4). Through selective survival, in which the superior groups fought their inferior neighbors, the species steadily improved, and after only seventy generations the next stage suddenly branched off (62:2.5-2.6).

062:44: In a treetop home an outstanding pair of dawn mammals gave birth to twins, a male and a female. Yet internal warfare once brought them to the brink of extinction, leaving a group of fewer than a hundred individuals (62:3.8).
